job: Standing up an in-house humanoid production fleet inside the manufacturer's own plants, justified against labor and downtime it already books on its own balance sheet

motivation: Captive demand and owned unit economics let it deploy internally without waiting for a per-robot rental price the open market will bear

task.when: Through 2026-2027 ramp toward the H1 2028 landing
task.why: Owned unit economics beat any open-market rental price
task.how: In-house Atlas-class humanoids run on the owner's balance sheet

job: Ramping humanoid manufacturing toward the stated ~25,000-unit 2028 target to supply its parent's captive in-house fleet rather than third-party RaaS customers
outcome: Verified at-scale unit volume exceeding low-thousands delivered into the owner's plants, making the captive fleet the largest reported paying production deployment
motivation: As a fully absorbed subsidiary its demand is its parent's plants, so volume goes inward before any external sale

task.who: the robot-maker's manufacturing and supply-chain operations team
task.what: Scale humanoid build rate toward the 25,000-unit target

job: Executing the ownership-consolidation buyout that absorbs the robot maker whole when the venture IPO exit fails, replacing market pricing with captive ownership
outcome: A closed acquisition that gives the owner 100% of the robot maker and the capital structure to deploy fleets internally rather than price them on the open market
motivation: Only an owner with capital and captive demand can absorb a robot maker, and the IPO-default put-option exit makes the asset acquirable
